content: This is an updated review of interventions aimed at increasing cervical screening uptake among women, building on the Cochrane review published in 2011. Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer affecting women globally, with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection being the causative factor in 99.7% of cases. Other risk factors include smoking, having multiple sexual partners, co-existing sexually transmitted infections, and immunosuppression. Primary prevention strategies focus on reducing HPV infection through vaccination, which has the potential to prevent nearly 90% of cases if administered before HPV exposure. However, vaccination programs are not universally accessible, and uptake remains poor in many countries. Consequently, secondary prevention through screening programs remains essential, particularly for unvaccinated women or those vaccinated later in adolescence. Screening aims to detect pre-cancerous cells and high-risk HPV. In the UK, the introduction of the Cervical Screening Programme in 1988 has significantly reduced cervical cancer mortality. However, globally, there is substantial variation in screening coverage and uptake. Some countries have national screening programs, while others rely on opportunistic screening. Within countries, disparities in screening uptake are influenced by factors such as ethnicity, age, education, and socioeconomic status. Addressing these factors in screening programs can improve participation rates, and when combined with vaccination, cervical cancer could become a rare disease. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to increase cervical screening uptake, including informed uptake. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of interventions aimed at improving screening participation. A comprehensive search of databases and other sources up to June 2020 identified 2597 records, of which 70 studies met the inclusion criteria. Sixty-nine trials, involving 257,899 participants, were included in a meta-analysis. The interventions assessed included invitations, educational materials, lay health worker involvement, counseling, and risk factor assessment. The evidence suggests that invitation letters are an effective method for increasing screening uptake compared to no intervention. Moderate-certainty evidence showed that personalized invitations, such as letters from general practitioners (GPs), fixed appointment letters, or personal invitations, were more effective than standard invitation letters. For example, fixed appointment letters were associated with higher uptake compared to open invitation letters (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.48 to 1.75; 5742 participants; 5 studies). Personalized invitations, such as telephone calls or face-to-face communication, also showed some benefit over standard letters (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.21; 27,663 participants; 5 studies). Low-certainty evidence supported the use of educational materials (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.18 to 1.54; 63,415 participants; 13 studies) and lay health worker involvement, particularly among ethnic minority populations (RR 2.30, 95% CI 1.44 to 3.65; 4330 participants; 11 studies). Other interventions, such as counseling, risk factor assessment, access to health promotion nurses, photo comic books, intensive recruitment efforts, and message framing, were less frequently studied. Sparse data and low-certainty evidence made it difficult to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness. However, access to health promotion nurses and intensive recruitment efforts may have contributed to increased screening uptake. One trial examined the economic impact of offering free screening compared to a fee-based approach. This trial, involving 3124 participants, found no significant difference in uptake at 90 days (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.03). The use of HPV self-testing as an alternative to conventional screening may also increase uptake, but this will be addressed in a subsequent review. Secondary outcomes, such as cost data, were incompletely reported. Many cluster-RCTs did not account for clustering or adequately report the number of clusters, limiting the ability to estimate the design effect. Despite these limitations, the overall conclusions and robustness of the results are unlikely to be significantly affected. However, considerable statistical heterogeneity was observed in the meta-analyses, and this should be considered when interpreting the findings. The certainty of evidence was downgraded due to unclear or high risk of bias in several trials, particularly regarding allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, and other methodological issues. In conclusion, moderate-certainty evidence supports the use of invitation letters to increase cervical screening uptake. Low-certainty evidence suggests that lay health worker involvement, particularly among ethnic minority populations, and educational interventions may also be beneficial, although the most effective format for educational materials remains unclear. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, limiting the generalizability of findings to lowand middle-income countries. Overall, the low-certainty evidence makes it challenging to determine the most effective interventions, except for invitational strategies, which appear to have more reliable evidence. Further research is needed to address these gaps and improve the evidence base.
